style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly.
chapterNote: Chapter 22 closes the long collection of Solomon's two-line proverbs (10:1-22:16) and then turns a corner. Verses 1-16 keep the familiar antithetic stamp, clustering around wealth and poverty, the LORD as Maker of rich and poor alike, the generous eye, the trained child, and the certainty that what a man sows in injustice he reaps in ruin. At verse 17 the voice changes: a fresh heading -- 'the words of the wise' -- opens the so-called 'Thirty Sayings' (vv. 17-21 frame them), summoning the son to bend his ear and lodge these truths on his lips so his trust may rest in the LORD. The chapter ends with the first of the thirty: do not exploit the poor or move the ancient boundary, for the LORD Himself takes their case -- and the man skilled at his work will stand before kings.

1.text: A good name is to be chosen above great riches, and to be held in loving favor counts for more than silver and gold.
1.amp: A good name [shem -- one's name, and so one's reputation and remembrance] is to be chosen [bachar -- preferred after weighing it out] above great riches, and loving favor [chen -- gracious regard, the goodwill others feel toward you] is better than silver [keseph] and gold [zahab].
1.notes: shem (H8034) is far more than a label -- it is the whole weight of a person's reputation and the memory left behind; bachar (H977) is deliberate, tested choice. The proverb weighs the intangible (a name, the favor of others) against the tangible (keseph H3701, zahab H2091) and declares the unseen worth more.

2.text: Rich and poor have this in common: the LORD is the Maker of them all.
2.amp: The rich [ashir -- the wealthy one] and the poor [rush -- the destitute] meet together [as equals on one level ground]; the LORD [YHWH] is the Maker [asah -- the One who made and fashioned] of them all.
2.notes: ashir (H6223) and rush (H7326) stand at opposite ends of fortune, yet share one Maker; asah (H6213) is to make or fashion. The leveling truth is theological, not merely sentimental -- both classes owe their existence to the same God (cf. Prov 29:13; Job 31:15), which forbids the rich any contempt and the poor any despair.

3.text: The prudent man sees trouble coming and takes cover, but the simple keep walking on and pay the penalty.
3.amp: The prudent [arum -- the shrewd, far-sighted one] foresees [raah -- sees, perceives] the evil [ra -- harm, calamity] and hides himself [satar -- conceals, takes cover], but the simple [peti -- the naive, easily-led] pass on [abar -- walk straight ahead] and are punished [anash -- pay the penalty, are fined].
3.notes: arum (H6175) is the same 'shrewd' once used of the serpent (Gen 3:1), here a virtue: the ability to read danger and act early. The contrast is not intelligence but attentiveness -- the peti (H6612) is not stupid so much as heedless, marching past warnings until the bill (anash, H6064) comes due (cf. Prov 27:12).

4.text: The reward of humility and the fear of the LORD is riches and honor and life.
4.amp: By humility [anavah -- lowliness, meekness before God] and the fear [yirah -- reverent awe] of the LORD [YHWH] come riches and honor [kavod -- weight, glory, esteem] and life [chay -- living, vitality].
4.notes: the chapter's wealth-language is here redeemed: the truest riches flow not from grasping but from anavah (H6038), humility, paired with yirat YHWH (H3374 + H3068), the book's master theme. kavod (H3519) is literally 'weight' -- the substance and honor of a settled life; the humble man, who claims nothing, is given everything (cf. Prov 18:12; Matt 5:5).

5.text: Thorns and snares lie along the road of the crooked; whoever guards his soul keeps far away from them.
5.amp: Thorns and snares are in the way [derek -- the road, the manner of life it carries] of the perverse [the twisted, crooked man]; he who guards [shamar -- keeps watch over, preserves] his soul [nephesh -- his life, his very self] stays far [rachaq -- keeps a wide distance] from them.
5.notes: the crooked man's derek (H1870) is booby-trapped with the consequences of his own bending; shamar (H8104) is sentry-keeping. To guard the nephesh (H5315) is to keep a deliberate, wide distance (rachaq, H7368) from that road -- safety lies in the route not taken (cf. Prov 4:14-15).

6.text: Train up a child according to the way he should go, and even when he is old he will not turn from it.
6.amp: Train up [chanak -- dedicate, initiate, set on a course] a child [naar -- a boy, youth] in the way [derek] he should go -- literally 'according to his way' -- and when he is old [zaqen -- aged] he will not depart [sur -- turn aside] from it.
6.notes: chanak (H2596) means to dedicate or initiate (the noun gives us Hanukkah, the dedication feast); the KJV margin even renders it 'catechize.' The Hebrew reads 'in his way,' which interpreters take as the way he ought to go or the bent of the child himself; either way, early formation lodges so deep that age (zaqen, H2204) will not pry it loose (sur, H5493).

7.text: The rich man rules over the poor, and the borrower becomes a slave to the one who lends.
7.amp: The rich [ashir] rules [mashal -- has dominion, governs] over the poor [rush], and the borrower [lavah -- one who has borrowed] is servant [ebed -- a slave, bondservant] to the man who lends [lavah -- literally 'the man of lending'].
7.notes: mashal (H4910) is to rule or dominate; ebed (H5650) is a bondservant. The proverb is sober observation, not approval: debt quietly transfers mastery, binding the borrower (lavah, H3867) to the lender. It warns the wise away from the chains of obligation (cf. Prov 22:26-27; Rom 13:8).

8.text: Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity, and the rod of his fury will be spent.
8.amp: He who sows [zara -- scatters seed] iniquity [avlah -- wickedness, injustice] will reap [qatsar -- harvest] trouble [aven -- emptiness, sorrow, wickedness], and the rod [shebet -- staff, scepter of authority] of his anger [evrah -- overflowing fury] will fail [kalah -- be finished, consumed, come to an end].
8.notes: the harvest law of Scripture: what is sown is reaped (zara H2232, qatsar H7114; cf. Gal 6:7; Hos 8:7). avlah (H5766) is injustice; aven (H205) is the hollow trouble it yields. The shebet (H7626) by which the oppressor lorded over others is itself spent and broken (kalah, H3615) -- the instrument of his cruelty consumes him.

9.text: The one with a generous eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.
9.amp: He who has a bountiful eye [literally 'good [tov] of eye' -- a generous, openhanded outlook] will be blessed [barak], for he gives [natan] of his bread [lechem -- food] to the poor [dal -- the weak, the lowly].
9.notes: the 'good eye' is a Hebrew idiom for generosity (its opposite, the 'evil eye,' is stinginess; cf. Prov 23:6; 28:22). tov (H2896) describes the open, kindly outlook that cannot keep its bread (lechem, H3899) while the dal (H1800) goes hungry; such a man is blessed (barak, H1288) in the very act of giving (cf. 2 Cor 9:6-8).

10.text: Drive out the scoffer, and strife goes out with him; quarrels and insults come to an end.
10.amp: Cast out [garash -- drive out, expel] the scorner [luts -- the mocker who sneers at correction], and contention [madon -- strife, discord] goes out; yes, quarreling [din -- legal dispute, wrangling] and reproach [qalon -- shame, insult] cease [shabat -- rest, stop].
10.notes: the lets/luts (H3887) is the scoffer, poison to any community; remove him (garash, H1644) and the strife he generates departs with him. The verbs pile up the relief -- madon (H4066), din (H1779), and qalon (H7036) all shabat (H7673), the very Sabbath-verb for ceasing. Peace is sometimes a matter of who is sent away (cf. Prov 26:20).

11.text: He who loves a pure heart and whose speech is gracious will have the king as his friend.
11.amp: He who loves [ahab] pureness [tahor -- cleanness, moral purity] of heart [leb], and whose lips [saphah -- speech] are gracious [chen -- full of grace and winsomeness], the king [melek] will be his friend [rea -- companion, intimate].
11.notes: two marks combine -- an inward tahor (H2889) heart and outward speech full of chen (H2580), grace. Such integrity wins even royal friendship: the melek (H4428) takes him as rea (H7453), a trusted companion. Inner purity and gracious words are not at odds; together they open the highest doors (cf. Prov 16:13; Ps 101:6).

12.text: The eyes of the LORD watch over knowledge, but He overturns the words of the treacherous.
12.amp: The eyes of the LORD [YHWH] preserve [natsar -- keep watch over, guard] knowledge [daat], but He overthrows [overturns, brings to nothing] the words [dabar -- the matters, plans] of the treacherous [bagad -- the faithless betrayer].
12.notes: God's watching eyes do double work: they natsar (H5341), guard and keep, true daat (H1847), while subverting the schemes (dabar, H1697) of the bagad (H898), the one who deals treacherously. Providence is not neutral -- it actively shelters truth and frustrates faithlessness (cf. Prov 15:3; 21:30).

13.text: The sluggard says, 'There is a lion outside! I will be murdered in the streets!'
13.amp: The sluggard [atsel -- the lazy one] says [amar], 'There is a lion [aryeh] outside [chuts -- out in the street]! I shall be slain [ratsach -- murdered] in the midst [tavek] of the streets!'
13.notes: atsel (H6102) is the sluggard, here painting an absurd excuse: a lion (aryeh, H738) prowling the open street (chuts, H2351) so he dare not go to work. ratsach (H7523) is the verb for unlawful killing -- he dramatizes his own murder to justify his bed. Laziness is endlessly inventive with reasons (cf. Prov 26:13).

14.text: The mouth of the forbidden woman is a deep pit; the man under the LORD's wrath falls into it.
14.amp: The mouth [peh -- speech] of the strange women [zur -- the foreign, off-limits woman] is a deep pit [a steep cistern with no escape]; he who is abhorred [zaam -- under the indignation] of the LORD [YHWH] falls [naphal -- drops, is brought down] into it.
14.notes: her peh (H6310) -- her flattering speech, not merely her body -- is the deep pit, echoing the 'smooth-tongued stranger' of chapter 2. The man already under God's za'am (H2194), His settled indignation, is the one who naphal (H5307), falls in; the trap and the judgment meet. The seductress's danger is finally a moral and divine reality (cf. Prov 2:16-19; 5:3-5).

15.text: Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of correction will drive it far from him.
15.amp: Foolishness [ivvelet -- moral folly, not mere ignorance] is bound up [tied fast] in the heart [leb] of a child [naar], but the rod [shebet] of correction [musar -- formative discipline] drives it far [rachaq -- removes to a distance] from him.
15.notes: ivvelet (H200) is folly as a bent of the will, not a gap in information -- it is knotted into the child's heart from the start. The shebet (H7626) of musar (H4148), loving corrective discipline, is the means by which it is driven away (rachaq, H7368). Correction is not cruelty but rescue from an inborn waywardness (cf. Prov 13:24; 29:15; Heb 12:11).

16.text: He who oppresses the poor to enrich himself, and he who gives to the rich -- both come only to want.
16.amp: He who oppresses [ashaq -- extorts, exploits] the poor [dal -- the weak, lowly] to increase [rabah -- multiply] his own, and he who gives to the rich [ashir] -- both come only to poverty [machsor -- want, lack].
16.notes: two grasping strategies, one ruin: ashaq (H6231) is to wring profit from the helpless dal (H1800), while the other fawns on the ashir (H6223), buying favor with the powerful. The closing word machsor (H4270) -- want -- falls on both; greed that exploits the weak and flattery that courts the strong arrive together at the same empty end (cf. Prov 28:8).

17.text: Bend your ear and listen to the words of the wise; set your heart on my knowledge.
17.amp: Bow down [natah -- stretch, incline] your ear [ozen] and hear [shama -- listen and heed] the words [dabar] of the wise [chakam -- the skilled, discerning]; apply [shith -- set, fix] your heart [leb] to my knowledge [daat].
17.notes: the voice shifts here, opening a new collection ('the words of the wise,' vv. 17-24:22). natah (H5186), to bend the ear, and shith (H7896), to set the heart, ask the whole person to lean in -- the same total posture urged in 2:2. shama (H8085) is hearing that obeys; the chakam (H2450) speaks, but only the leb (H3820) that fixes itself on the daat (H1847) truly receives.

18.text: For it is a pleasant thing to keep them deep within you, to have them all ready upon your lips.
18.amp: For it is pleasant [naim -- sweet, delightful] if you keep [shamar -- guard, store] them within [beten -- the belly, the innermost self]; let them all be fixed together [kun -- established, made ready] on your lips [saphah].
18.notes: naim (H5273) is sweetness and delight -- wisdom kept is not a burden but a pleasure. The teaching is to be lodged in the beten (H990), the inmost being, and from that depth made ready (kun, H3559) on the saphah (H8193), the lips -- truth stored within becomes speech without; what fills the heart is what comes out of the mouth (cf. Matt 12:34).

19.text: That your trust may rest in the LORD, I have taught you this very day -- yes, you.
19.amp: That your trust [mivtach -- confidence, secure reliance] may be in the LORD [YHWH], I have made known [yada -- caused you to know] to you this day [yom], even to you.
19.notes: here is the aim of all the teaching: not mere cleverness but mivtach (H4009), settled trust, anchored in YHWH alone. yada (H3045) is to make truly known. The doubled 'even to you' presses it home as personal address -- this wisdom is not for someone else but for you, today (cf. Prov 3:5-6).

20.text: Is it not true that I have written out for you these thirty noble things -- guidance and knowledge alike --
20.amp: Have I not written for you excellent things -- thirty sayings -- of counsel [moetsah -- guidance, plans] and knowledge [daat],
20.notes: the Hebrew shalishim is read as 'thirty,' the number of distinct sayings in this section (echoing the Egyptian 'Instruction of Amenemope,' which had thirty chapters), or as 'excellent/noble things.' Either way the gift is moetsah (H4156), wise counsel, and daat (H1847), knowledge -- a deliberate, ordered body of teaching, not random advice.

21.text: to teach you what is certain and true, so that you can give a reliable answer to those who send you?
21.amp: to make you know the certainty [qoshet -- truth, what is firm and reliable] of the words [emer -- sayings] of truth [emeth -- faithfulness, dependability], so that you may answer [shub -- bring back a reply] words of truth to those who send [shalach -- dispatch] you?
21.notes: qoshet (H7189) and emeth (H571) pile up the idea of solid reliability -- wisdom that does not shift under the feet. The purpose is practical and public: to equip the learner to shub (H7725), return a true and tested report, to those who shalach (H7971), send him out. Wisdom received is meant to be wisdom relayed, faithful in the messenger's mouth.

22.text: Do not rob the poor because he is poor, and do not crush the afflicted in the gate,
22.amp: Do not rob [gazal -- seize by force, tear away] the poor [dal] because he is poor, nor crush [oppress, grind down] the afflicted [ani -- the humble sufferer] in the gate [shaar -- the city gate, the seat of justice].
22.notes: the first of the thirty sayings. gazal (H1497) is violent, forcible robbery -- and to do it precisely because a man is dal (H1800), too weak to resist, is doubly vile. The shaar (H8179), the city gate, was the courtroom of ancient Israel; to crush the ani (H6041) there is to corrupt justice at its source, the very abuse the prophets thundered against (cf. Amos 5:12; Zech 7:10).

23.text: for the LORD will take up their cause, and He will plunder the life of those who plunder them.
23.amp: for the LORD [YHWH] will plead [rib -- contend, argue the legal case] their cause [riyb -- their lawsuit, their dispute], and He will despoil [plunder, strip] the soul [nephesh -- the very life] of those who despoiled them.
23.notes: the reason the poor must not be wronged: the LORD Himself steps into court as their Advocate. rib (H7378) is to litigate, to argue a case; God takes up the riyb (H7379) of the helpless as His own. The exact retribution -- He plunders the nephesh (H5315) of the plunderers -- makes the oppression of the weak a direct provocation of God (cf. Prov 23:11; Ps 68:5).

24.text: Do not make friends with a hot-tempered man, and do not go about with one given to fury,
24.amp: Make no friendship with an angry [aph -- literally 'nose,' the flaring of wrath] master [baal -- an owner, one possessed by his anger], and with a furious [chemah -- hot, burning wrath] man [ish] you shall not go [bo -- enter in, keep company],
24.notes: aph (H639), wrath, comes from the word for the nose -- the flared nostril of rage; he is a baal (H1167), literally an 'owner' of anger, mastered by it. chemah (H2534) is burning fury. The warning is against companionship itself (bo, H935) with such a man, for character is contagious (cf. Prov 13:20; 1 Cor 15:33).

25.text: or you will learn his ways and lay a snare for your own soul.
25.amp: lest you learn [alaph -- become familiar with, get accustomed to] his ways [orach -- paths, habits], and take [laqach -- get, fetch] a snare [moqesh -- trap, bait] to your soul [nephesh].
25.notes: alaph (H502) is to learn by close association until a habit is absorbed -- the danger named in v. 24 spelled out. The angry man's orach (H734), his settled patterns, rub off; the one who keeps such company laqach (H3947), fetches, a moqesh (H4170) -- a baited trap -- for his own nephesh (H5315). We come to resemble what we walk beside.

26.text: Do not be one of those who give their hand in pledge, who put up security for another's debts.
26.amp: Do not be among those who strike hands [taqa -- clap the hand, the gesture sealing a pledge], among those who become surety [arab -- guarantee, pledge themselves] for debts [mashshaah -- loans, what is owed].
26.notes: to taqa (H8628) the hand was to seal a guarantee with a handshake -- ancient cosigning. arab (H6148) is to pledge oneself as surety for another's debt. Proverbs repeatedly warns against it (6:1-5; 11:15; 17:18): not because generosity is wrong, but because binding your livelihood to another's obligations can hand your very bed to a creditor -- as the next verse shows.

27.text: If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your very bed be taken from under you?
27.amp: If you have nothing to pay [shalam -- to make whole, settle the debt], why should he take [laqach -- seize] your bed [mishkab -- the place where you lie] from under you?
27.notes: shalam (H7999), to repay, shares its root with shalom -- to settle a debt is to make things whole again. But the cosigner with empty hands has nothing to make whole; the creditor then takes the mishkab (H4904), the very bed beneath him -- the last and most basic possession (cf. Exod 22:26-27). Folly in a pledge can cost a man the ground he sleeps on.

28.text: Do not move the ancient boundary stone that your fathers set in place.
28.amp: Do not remove [nasag -- shift back, displace] the ancient [olam -- long-standing, from of old] landmark [gevul -- boundary marker, property line] which your fathers [ab] set up [asah -- made, established].
28.notes: the gevul (H1366) was the boundary stone marking inherited land; to move it secretly was a form of theft, stealing acreage by stealth, and is cursed in the Law (Deut 19:14; 27:17). Calling it olam (H5769), ancient, and tracing it to the ab (H1 -- the fathers) frames it as a sacred trust handed down -- a reverence for inherited boundaries, both literal and moral, that one generation owes the next.

29.text: Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will stand before kings; he will not stand before obscure men.
29.amp: Do you see [chazah -- behold, observe with discernment] a man [ish] diligent [skilled, quick and practiced] in his work [melakah -- his craft, his occupation]? He will stand [yatsab -- take his stand, present himself] before kings [melek]; he will not stand before obscure [chashok -- dim, lowly, undistinguished] men.
29.notes: chazah (H2372) is to look with insight, inviting the reader to notice a pattern of life. The mahir -- the skilled, practiced workman -- at his melakah (H4399) does not need to push for advancement; competence itself promotes him to yatsab (H3320), stand before kings (melek, H4428), not before chashok (H2823), the dim and obscure. Excellence quietly opens its own doors (cf. Prov 12:24; Gen 41:46).
